title: Follow the money: Van Nelle
summary: Everything in this house was paid for by tobacco, coffee and tea. Albertus Sonneveld worked at Van Nelle for fifty years, rising from clerk to director of the tobacco division.

life.text: Van Nelle began in 1782 as a Rotterdam shop selling coffee, tea and tobacco. In the 19th century it became a factory business processing raw materials, partly from plantations on Java.

Sonneveld joined in 1900, aged fourteen, trained in the tobacco trade and travelled to America for the first time at twenty-four. As director he spent months each year in the United States buying tobacco and arranging its shipment.
Van Nelle’s architects, Brinkman & Van der Vlugt, who had just completed the Van Nelle Factory, designed the house and its complete interior. The family moved in in 1933.
The Nieuwe Instituut’s research project Collecting Otherwise names Sonneveld House as a case study, including “Sonneveld’s tobacco histories in Paducah USA and the plantations in Indonesia”.

materials.source: Bought in the American South and from the Dutch East Indies (Indonesia).
Plantation crops from Java and elsewhere in the Dutch colonial empire.

questions: Which plantations supplied Van Nelle in the years Sonneveld was director, and who worked on them?

title: Seascape with two botters
summary: Above the sofa hung a seascape with two botters, traditional Dutch fishing boats. The Sonnevelds paired avant-garde furniture with fairly traditional painting.

life.text: Painted by W.B. Tholen, a painter close to the Hague School, who died in 1931.
Hung above the living-room sofa, the main wall of the room.
Photographed for the museum’s Art and design pages.

materials.source: No direct colonial source identified.
Bought from a salary earned in Van Nelle’s trade in tobacco, coffee and tea (see “Follow the money”).

title: The grand piano
summary: The grand piano is already drawn into the architects’ design for the living room. Its place was fixed before the house was built.

life.text: Drawn into Brinkman & Van der Vlugt’s interior design for the living room (archive BROX 93t21).
Stands in the living room, next to the sofa and the seascape.
The design drawing is in the Brinkman & Van der Vlugt archive at the Nieuwe Instituut.

materials.source: Piano keys of this period were usually covered in elephant ivory, much of it auctioned in Antwerp and London from colonial Central and East Africa. Not yet verified for this instrument.
A tropical hardwood, typically from Central Africa or South and Southeast Asia. Not yet verified for this instrument.

title: Lion
summary: A seated lion by John Rädecker, one of the leading Dutch sculptors between the wars. It stands next to the piano on a pedestal designed by Brinkman & Van der Vlugt.

life.text: Made in 1925. In the early 1920s Rädecker made similar animal figures for the collector Helene Kröller-Müller. The archive names Art Nouveau, Cubism and non-European art among his early influences.
The family owned two works by Rädecker: this lion, next to the piano, and a mask from 1924, said to be a portrait study of Puck, in the staircase.
The original left the house with the family. During the restoration it was traced to one of the Sonnevelds’ grandsons.
A cast was taken from the original, and the lion in the house today is a cast-stone replica. Glass negatives in the collection show it in the living room.

materials.source: Cast from the original during the restoration.
The archive names non-European art among Rädecker’s early influences. Which works he drew on, and how he saw them, for example in colonial or ethnographic collections, is not documented here.
Bought from a salary earned in Van Nelle’s trade in tobacco, coffee and tea (see “Follow the money”).

questions: What is the original made of, and where is it now?

title: Cantilever chair with woven seat
summary: A tubular steel cantilever chair with a woven seat and back. Cane and rattan reached Dutch furniture makers mainly from the Dutch East Indies.

life.text: Rattan palms grow wild in the forests of Kalimantan, Sulawesi and Sumatra, where it was gathered and traded through ports such as Banjarmasin and Surabaya.
Cantilever chairs with woven seats were made in series by firms such as Thonet. Sketches for the interior from 1932 often mention Thonet furniture.
Stands in the living room, in front of the piano.

materials.source: Commercial rattan came mostly from Indonesia, then the Dutch East Indies.
In 1931 Southern Rhodesia (a British colony) supplied 37% of the world’s chromite exports and New Caledonia (a French colony) 16%.

questions: Is this an original Sonneveld piece, and who made it?

title: Tubular steel armchairs
summary: Serial tubular steel furniture and lamps by Gispen define the modern interior. The architects chose them from Gispen’s catalogues.

life.text: Gispen sold standardised tubular steel furniture through illustrated catalogues, such as no. 52.
The museum collection includes Gispen armchairs no. 407 and 408 from 1933.
The Gispen catalogues are part of the Gispen archive at the Nieuwe Instituut.

materials.source: European steel.
In 1931 Southern Rhodesia (a British colony) supplied 37% of the world’s chromite exports and New Caledonia (a French colony) 16%.

title: The carpet
summary: The archive records a Moroccan carpet bought from Metz & Co, the Amsterdam shop for modern interiors.

life.text: Hand-knotted wool carpets were made by Amazigh (Berber) weavers in Morocco, then a French protectorate (1912–1956).
Metz & Co sold such carpets alongside modern furniture, lamps and Van der Leck fabrics.
A carpet of this kind lay in the living area.
Metz & Co folders and catalogues survive in the E. Berkovich archive at the Nieuwe Instituut.

materials.source: Morocco, under French colonial rule. Modernist interiors embraced these carpets, usually without their makers’ names.

title: Light without shadows
summary: The family chose 22 different lamps from Giso catalogue no. 29 (1929). The opal glass spreads the light evenly, without glare or hard shadows.

life.text: Gispen developed its own Giso glass for diffused light.
Ceiling lamps light the living room and library.
The Giso catalogue of 1929 is in the Gispen archive at the Nieuwe Instituut.

materials.source: No colonial source identified yet.

title: The ribbon window
summary: A steel frame carries the house, so the façade could open up into long bands of glass and the rooms could flow into each other.

life.text: The architects applied the steel-frame construction they had developed for the Van Nelle Factory.
The window runs along the living room and the library.
Piet Zwart photographed the room in 1933.

materials.source: European industry. No direct colonial source identified.

title: Desk and yellow chair
summary: In 1933 Mrs Sonneveld’s small desk stood by the window: Bruno Weil’s tubular steel B91. The yellow chair is one of Van der Leck’s colour accents.

life.text: Designed by Bruno Weil in 1931. Sketches from 1932 often mention furniture by the German-Austrian firm Thonet.
Piet Zwart’s 1933 photograph shows the desk at the window of the sitting room.
Vermilion, cornflower blue and yolk yellow appear as accents among bronze, brown and beige.

materials.source: In 1931 Southern Rhodesia (a British colony) supplied 37% of the world’s chromite exports and New Caledonia (a French colony) 16%.

title: The library
maker: Orange-red armchairs; portrait attributed to Jozef Israëls

life.text: A curtain divides the library from the living room, so the two can be one space.
Vases by A.D. Copier from the Leerdam glassworks stood in the library and sitting room.
Glass negatives in the collection show the vases in place.

title: Colour on large surfaces
maker: Bart van der Leck, fabrics by Metz & Co
summary: In the bedrooms Van der Leck’s colours cover large surfaces. Sonneveld House is the earliest known Dutch interior to use his fabrics for Metz & Co.

life.text: Van der Leck’s palette: vermilion, cornflower blue and yolk yellow, with light grey, dark grey and brown.
The fabrics came from Metz & Co’s new sample book in Van der Leck’s colours.
Metz & Co material survives in the E. Berkovich archive.

materials.source: Fibre and dye sources not yet researched.
